questiontext.text: In which temperature range is the occurrence of Supercooled Liquid Water (SLW) MOST frequent and significant for structural icing?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: SLW is most prevalent between 0°C and -15°C. Below -20°C, the probability of spontaneous freezing into ice crystals increases significantly, reducing the available liquid water for icing.

questiontext.text: Why is Glaze (Clear) ice considered more hazardous than Rime ice for aircraft operations?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Glaze ice is hard, transparent, and heavy. Because it forms from larger droplets or high liquid water content, it often "runs back" and freezes on surfaces behind the leading edge that are not protected by de-icing boots or heaters.

answer.text: It is heavier and can spread to unprotected areas aft of the leading edge.
It is more brittle and breaks off into the engines.
It only forms in clear air where it cannot be seen.
It creates more drag than weight penalty.

questiontext.text: Which thermodynamic structure is required for the formation of Freezing Rain (FZRA) at the surface?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: FZRA requires a melting layer (T > 0°C) above a sub-freezing layer (T < 0°C) near the surface. Snow melts in the warm layer and becomes supercooled rain in the cold layer below.

answer.text: A warm layer above 0°C overlying a sub-freezing layer near the ground.
A constant lapse rate of 6.5°C per km from the surface upward.
An absolute instability from the surface to the tropopause.

questiontext.text: When analyzing a sounding for icing potential, which combination of parameters indicates the HIGHEST risk?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: High icing risk is associated with saturated layers (dewpoint depression < 5°C) within the critical temperature range (0°C to -15°C), especially if the layer is unstable (convective), which implies higher liquid water content.

answer.text: Temperature -8°C, Dewpoint Depression 2°C, and Unstable Lapse Rate.
Temperature -25°C, Dewpoint Depression 1°C, and Stable Lapse Rate.
